title: Death as a work of nature
word: Death as a work of nature
hook: death is like teething, growing up, having children: one of nature's works (Meditations 9.3)

segments.voice: Yesterday: for one another, and one small wrong set right. Your line was for one another. Did you pull a thread straight? Day six hundred seven.

A baby is cutting teeth: fussy, drooling, awake at three in the morning. Nobody calls it a tragedy. It's hard, it hurts, and everyone in the house knows it's just what babies do on the way to growing up. Marcus picks up exactly that ordinary picture, teething, and sets it beside something we usually treat very differently. Gently, because it's a tender subject, today we read his thought on dying. Today: death as a work of nature.
screen: `A BABY CUTTING TEETH.` → `HARD, BUT NATURAL.` → `DEATH AS A WORK OF NATURE.`

segments.voice: First, the list. In book nine Marcus writes: don't despise death, but be content with it, since it's one of the things nature wills. Then he names the others. Being young and growing old. Growing up and reaching full size. Getting teeth, a beard, gray hair. Conceiving, carrying a child, giving birth. All the works our seasons of life bring. Dying, he says, belongs on the same list. Second, the pace. He doesn't say rush toward it, and he doesn't say ignore it. He says wait for it the way you'd wait for a child to be born: not anxious, not careless, knowing it comes in its own time. That, he says, is how a thoughtful person meets it. Third, a plainer comfort. Then Marcus does something surprising. He offers a homelier consolation, the kind that reaches the heart: think of the things you'll leave, and the habits of the people you'll no longer have to live among. But in the same breath he checks himself. Don't be offended with them, he writes. Care for them, and bear with them gently. Fourth, what this is and isn't. This is a Stoic view, and not everyone holds it. Many traditions speak of death in terms of a soul, a judgment, a world to come, or rebirth, and Marcus himself, across the book, is unsure what follows. What he offers here isn't a teaching about the afterlife. It's a posture: to see dying as part of the same nature that brought teeth and gray hair, and so not to meet it with horror.
screen: `TEETH, GRAY HAIR, BIRTH, DEATH.` · `WAIT AS FOR A BIRTH.` · `A HOMELIER COMFORT, CHECKED.` · `A POSTURE, NOT A DOCTRINE.` · then, large: `NATURE'S WORK.`

segments.voice: This one is gentle. Settle, and breathe. If this subject is tender for you right now, simply rest with the breath; that's enough. Otherwise, bring to mind the changes your body has already lived through: first teeth, a growth spurt, a first gray hair, maybe a pregnancy or a child. Each one arrived on its own schedule. Let the thought sit quietly beside them: my life has a shape, and an ending is part of the shape. Don't push it. Just breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
Death as a work of nature. Marcus sets dying on the same list as teething, growing up and gray hair: one of nature's works, waited for, not dreaded. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: nature's work. When you notice something changing in your body today, a gray hair, a stiff knee, say nature's work, and let it be ordinary. Day six hundred seven.

howItsDone: Stoic readers often reflect briefly on mortality as part of nature's ordinary course, alongside growing up and growing old, as a way of meeting it calmly rather than with dread.

fork.setup: you're Marcus, and the thought of death comes up. how does he tell himself to meet it?
options: dread it as the worst thing.
wait for it as one of nature's works, like a birth.
fork.reveal: he says neither despise it nor dread it: wait for it the way you'd wait for a child to be born.

original.note: Greek: nature, the way things grow. Marcus calls dying one of the works of physis.

trapdoor: what you thought: a stern Stoic saying death doesn't matter.
what it means: Marcus puts dying alongside teething and gray hair, and waits for it calmly, neither scorning it nor dreading it.
what a scholar hears: the entry gives a reasoned consolation, then a plainer one Marcus marks as less philosophical, and checks it at once with a call to gentleness.

notes: 9.3 paraphrased: do not despise death but be content with it as one of the things nature wills (youth, age, growth, teeth, beard, gray hairs, begetting, pregnancy, birth); wait for it as for the child to come from the womb; the 'common' (Long: 'vulgar') comfort that reaches the heart: the objects you leave and the manners of those you no longer live among; yet do not be offended with them but care for them and bear with them gently. Confirm.
